accepted.question_text: Is every topological group a quotient group of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight? More specifically, when a topological group is almost metrizable, meaning that it contains a compact subset of countable character, under what additional conditions is it a quotient of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight?

evidence.quote: Problem 1 (Choban). Is every topological group a quotient group of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight? When an almost metrizable topological group is a quotient of a zero-dimensional group of the same weight?
A space X is zero-dimensional if dim X = 0. A topological group is almost metrizable if contains a compact subset of countable character.

accepted.question_text: For a metrizable space X, under which conditions is the free universal algebra of an uncountable signature over X paracompact? In particular, if L(X) denotes the free topological linear space over X over the discrete field of real numbers, is L(X) paracompact?

evidence.quote: Problem 2 (Choban). Under which conditions is the free universal algebra of an uncountable signature over a metrizable space X paracompact? In particular, is the free topological linear space L(X) of X over the discrete field of real numbers paracompact?

accepted.question_text: Let X be a zero-dimensional compact homogeneous topological space. Let S(X) be the semigroup of all continuous self-maps of X, viewed as a subsemigroup of X^X with the topology of pointwise convergence. A semigroup with identity e is called left bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F such that the whole semigroup equals F U. Must S(X) be left bounded for every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space X?

evidence.quote: A semigroup S with the identity e endowed with a topology is called a left (resp. right) bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F of S such that S = F U (resp. S = UF); S is called bounded if S is both left and right bounded.

For a topological space X let S(X) ⊂ XX be the semigroup of all continuous self-mappings of X endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence (i.e., the topology inherited from the Tychonov product XX). A topological space X is called homogeneous if for any points x1, x2 ∈ X there is a homemorphism h of X with h(x1) = x2.
Problem 3 (Protasov). Is the semigroup S(X) left bounded for every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space?

accepted.question_text: Let X be a zero-dimensional homogeneous topological space, and let S(X) be the semigroup of all continuous self-maps of X with the topology of pointwise convergence. A semigroup with identity e is called right bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F such that the whole semigroup equals U F. Must S(X) be right bounded for every zero-dimensional homogeneous space X?

evidence.quote: A semigroup S with the identity e endowed with a topology is called a left (resp. right) bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F of S such that S = F U (resp. S =UF); S is called bounded if S is both left and right bounded.

For a topological space X let S(X) ⊂ XX be the semigroup of all continuous self-mappings of X endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence (i.e., the topology inherited from the Tychonov product XX). A topological space X is called homogeneous if for any points x1, x2 ∈ X there is a homemorphism h of X with h(x1) = x2.
Problem 4 (Protasov). Is the semigroup S(X) right bounded for any zero-dimensional homogeneous space X?

accepted.question_text: Let X be a compact topological space, and let H be a subgroup of S(X), the semigroup of continuous self-maps of X. Suppose H acts transitively on X and is distal, meaning that for any distinct points x1 and x2 in X and any point x in X there exists a neighborhood U of x such that {h(x1), h(x2)} is not contained in U for all h in H. Must H be left bounded?

evidence.quote: Let X be a topological space. A subgroup H of S(X) is called distal if for any distinct points x1, x2 ∈ X and any point x ∈ X there is a neighborhood U of x such that {h(x1), h(x2)} 6⊂ U for all h ∈ H.
Problem 5 (Protasov). Let X be a compact space and H be a distal subgroup of S(X), acting transitively on X. Is H left bounded?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a bounded semitopological group or a bounded quasitopological group. Here bounded means that for every neighborhood U of the identity there is a finite subset F with G = F U and also G = U F. A semitopological group is a group whose topology is invariant under both left and right shifts, and a quasitopological group is a semitopological group with continuous inversion. Must every such bounded semitopological group, and every such bounded quasitopological group, have countable cellularity?

evidence.quote: A semigroup S with the identity e endowed with a topology is called a left (resp. right) bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F of S such that S = F U (resp. S =UF); S is called bounded if S is both left and right bounded.

If, in addition τ is invariant with respect to the right shifts, then (G, τ ) is called a semitopological group. A semitopological group G with continuous inverse mapping x 7→ x−1 is called a quasitopological group.
Problem 6 (Protasov). Let G be a bounded semitopological (quasitopological) group. Has G countable cellularity?

accepted.question_text: Does every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space admit a left-topological group structure? Equivalently, if a compact space is zero-dimensional and homogeneous, must there exist a group operation on its underlying set together with a topology invariant under all left shifts x ↦ g x? In particular, if K is a first-countable zero-dimensional compact space, does its countable power K^ω admit the structure of a left-topological group?
accepted.context_brief: Left-topological group structures on homogeneous compacta

evidence.quote: Under a left-topological group we understand a pair (G, τ ) consisting of a group G and a topology τ invariant with respect to the left shifts lg : x 7→ gx.

Problem 7 (Protasov). Does every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space admit the structure of a left topological group? In particular, does the countable power Kω of a first-countable zero-dimensional compact space K admit the structure of a left topological group?
This problem was answered in negative by Banakh in [T.Banakh, A homogeneous first-countable zero-dimensional compactum failing to be a left-topological group, Mat. Stud.29 (2008) 215–217].

accepted.question_text: Let G be a compact left-topological group, meaning a group endowed with a topology invariant under all left shifts. Must G support a strictly positive probability Borel measure, that is, a Borel probability measure μ such that μ(U) > 0 for every nonempty open subset U of G?

evidence.quote: Under a left-topological group we understand a pair (G, τ ) consisting of a group G and a topology τ invariant with respect to the left shifts lg : x 7→ gx.
while compact topological groups support a strictly positive probability measure (i.e., a Borel probability measure µ such that µ(U) > 0 for any nonempty open subset U of the group).
Problem 8 (Protasov). Does every compact left topological group G support a strictly positive probability Borel measure?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a paratopological group. Suppose G is right ω-bounded, meaning that for every neighborhood U of the identity there exists a countable subset F of G such that G = U F. Must G also be left ω-bounded, meaning that for every neighborhood U of the identity there exists a countable subset F of G such that G = F U?

evidence.quote: A paratopological group G is left ω-bounded (resp. right ω-bounded) if for any neighborhood U ⊂ G of the origin there is a countable subset F ⊂ G with G = F U (resp. G = UF); G is ω-bounded if it is both left and right ω-bounded.
Problem 10 (Guran). Is a paratopological group G left ω-bounded if it is right ω-bounded?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a metrizable topological group G that is o-bounded, meaning that for every sequence (U_n) of neighborhoods of the identity there is a sequence (F_n) of finite subsets of G such that G is contained in the union of the sets F_n U_n, and for which Player I nevertheless has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)? In this game, at each stage n, Player I chooses a neighborhood U_n of the identity and Player II chooses a finite subset F_n of G; Player II wins exactly when G is contained in the union of the sets F_n U_n.
accepted.context_brief: O-bounded groups and the OF game

evidence.quote: A subset A of a topological group G is called o-bounded if for any sequence (Un)n∈ω of neighborhoods of the origin of G there is a sequence (Fn)n∈ω of finite subsets of G such that A ⊂ S n∈ω FnUn.

Two players, I and II, choose at every step k ∈ ω a neighborhood Un ⊂ G of the origin, and a finite subset Fn of G, respectively. At the end of the game, the player II is declared the winner if A ⊂ S n∈ω FnUn.
Problem 11 (Banakh). Is there a (metrizable) o-bounded topological group G such that the player I has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)?

accepted.question_text: Let A be a compact subset of the real line R such that the difference set A − A = {a − a′ : a, a′ ∈ A} is a neighborhood of 0 in R. Must the fourfold sumset A + A + A + A have nonempty interior in R?

evidence.quote: Problem 12 (Banakh). Let A be a compact subset of the real line R such that A − A = {a−a′ : a, a′ ∈ A} is a neighborhood of zero in R. Has the sum A+A+A+A non-empty interior in R?
